newsitem.title: USA: Many Watergate players are still on the stage.
newsitem.headline: Many Watergate players are still on the stage.

text.p: Many of the actors in the Watergate drama are still basking in the limelight 25 years later with, oddly enough, two bit players -- once young lawyers Hillary Rodham Clinton and Fred Thompson -- occupying centre stage in Washington.
Other players in the drama of cover-up and political foul play have found God, the presidential campaign trail, show business and law offices where they can sue each other.
Many, of course, have passed away or disappeared in obscurity.

Clinton is first lady of the land and Thompson a powerful Republican senator from Tennessee about to probe how her president husband financed his re-election and whether foreign governments and businesses made illegal contributions.
During Watergate, Mrs Clinton was a lawyer for the Democrats on the House of Representatives Impeachment Committee and Thompson was a lawyer for the Republican side on the Senate Watergate committee.
"What goes around, comes around," said Monica Crowley, President Richard Nixon's assistant in the last days of his life and the author of the best-seller "Nixon Off the Record."
Nixon died at age 81 in 1994, with millions thinking of him as an elder statesman and glossing over the fact he was the only president ever to resign from the office.
Crowley said that at the end of his life, Nixon deeply regretted his role in accelerating "the crisis of mistrust in this country toward government and its institutions."

She is currently working on a book on his final thoughts on Watergate which will be published next year and says it will contain "many revelations about what happened and why." The implication is clear -- 25 years later the truth is out there to be discovered just like the identity of "Deep Throat," the source for the Washington Post on many of the key breaks of the scandal.

Other key figures in the scandal who have died include ex-Attorney General John Mitchell, his talkative ex-wife Martha, senior White House aide H.R. Haldeman and courtly Democrat Sam Ervin, who chaired the Watergate hearings.
Here is an update on some of other figures who took part:

-- Pat Buchanan, Nixon speechwriter who, while not involved in the scandal, defended the president. Today, he talks about his two runs for the presidency and the 15th anniversary of his CNN television talk show "Crossfire," which pits liberals and conservatives in bloody verbal battle and revolutionised the discussion of politics on TV.

But of Watergate, he says, "The lesson is don't send Cubans in without air cover." This was a reference to the anti-Castro Cubans who took part in the break-in at Democratic National headquarters on June 17, 1972.

-- Charles Colson, Nixon's special counsel who spent almost a year in jail for obstructing justice, is now a born-again Christian counselling prisoners. Four years ago, he won a $1 million religion prize for his work.

-- John Dean, the White House counsel who turned into Nixon's chief accuser, warning him that there was "cancer on the presidency." Dean is now an investment banker and is involved in law suits against Watergate conspirator G. Gordon Liddy, who claims Dean masterminded the whole thing.

Dean said, "My reflection on it over the years has been, I was very young when I went there, I was not trained in the criminal law. I didn't think that was a criteria to be counsel to the president. It seems to be one of the sad legacies of the past for the job. It's had a permanent impact."

-- G. Gordon Liddy, the campaign offical who served four years in jail, is now a radio talk show host and lecture circuit speaker who teamed up with Timothy Leary and Abbie Hoffman to entertain college audiences. Proud that he was the conspirator who wouldn't talk, Liddy now says the truth about Watergate has to be told and claims Dean was behind it all. "The full truth has to be told. ... I want to go to trial. The public perception about what happened is incorrect."

-- Washington Post publisher Katherine Graham is now of the most repected figures in American journalism and the author of a widely-praised memoir. She says, "Sometimes people accuse us of 'bringing down a president,' which of course we didn't do and shouldn't have done. The processes that caused his resignation were constitutional...

"What the Post did and the press did was keep the story alive in the summer months, through the election, when they were trying to hush it up, and they were really pulling all the stops to hush it up."

-- Washington Post reporter Bob Woodward is still with the paper breaking scoops while his Watergate partner Carl Bernstein is a freelance writer whose latest book credits the Pope with "secretly" aiding the Reagan administration to bring down communism, a point of view that has been challenged by historians.
